Learning Objectives
Review the common ischemic pathway and pathophysiology of osteonecrosis of the hip.
Recognize risk factors predisposing patients to osteonecrosis of the hip.
Explain the natural history of unmanaged and managed hip osteonecrosis.
Recognize key imaging features of hip osteonecrosis on plain radiographs and MRIs.
Describe the 2019 Association Research Circulation Osseous classification system.
Differentiate hip osteonecrosis from hip conditions with a similar patient presentation,
including transient osteoporosis of the hip and femoral neck stress fractures.
List the indications for various surgical treatment options for hip osteonecrosis, including hip
preservation and total hip arthroplasty.
Recognize the role of adjuvant cell-based therapy and bone grafting after core decompression.

Pathophysiology
Overview
Nontraumatic osteonecrosis of the femoral head (NONFH) is a progressive and debilitating hip
disease that occurs in young and middle-aged adults.
A causative interaction exists between genetic predisposition, risk factor exposure, altered
bone cell physiology, and vascular impairment.
The exact pathophysiologic mechanism has not been established; however, a common
pathway in all causes of NONFH involves the microvascular circulation of the femoral head,
leading to ischemia.
NONFH is characterized by a pattern of ischemia, cell death, bone resorption, repair, and
subchondral collapse or fracture of the femoral head.
Impaired blood supply to the femoral head in osteonecrosis of the femoral head (ONFH) may
be secondary to vascular interruption, intravascular occlusion, or extravascular compression.
Increased bone marrow adiposity and edema is associated with increased femoral head
pressure. Adipogenesis is a pathophysiologic mechanism observed in patients with
glucocorticoid- and alcohol-associated NONFH.
Human bone marrow mesenchymal stems cells are multipotent cells that can differentiate into
various cells, including adipocytes and osteocytes. They play a role in the pathophysiology and
management of NONFH. 

Overview
NONFH is a complex, multifactorial, and progressive condition. The pathophysiologic
mechanism arises from an interaction between genetic predisposition, risk factor
exposure, altered bone cell physiology, and vascular impairment, leading to ischemia
and necrosis of bone.
The vascular anatomy and vulnerability of blood supply to the femoral head has been
well described.1 Disruption of the blood supply to the femoral head, leading to ischemia,
marrow necrosis, and osteocyte death, is a common pathway observed in patients with
NONFH. The mechanisms include intravascular occlusion from thrombi or embolic fat,
intraosseous extravascular compression, and extraosseous venous obstruction. Elevated


Epidemiology
The exact incidence and prevalence of NONFH in the United States remains unknown. A
large epidemiologic study from China included 30,030 subjects to determine the
prevalence of osteonecrosis of the hip. All participants underwent a medical history,
physical examination, lipid profiles, and imaging studies (radiographs and/or MRI). The
prevalence of NONFH in patients 15 years or older was 0.75%. The overall prevalence
independent of associated predisposing factors was higher in males (1.02%) than in
females (0.5%). NONFH in males more frequently was associated with heavy smoking
(21% in males versus 4% in females) and heavy drinking (33% in males versus 8% in
females). Glucocorticoids were more frequently associated in females with NONFH (56%)
than in males (26%).
In 2015, 46,745 surgical procedures were performed for ONFH in the United States. Most
surgical procedures performed were hip replacement procedures, such as THA (90%),
partial arthroplasty (7%), and resurfacing (0.2%). ONFH in the United States was rarely
managed via hip preservation surgical techniques. Nonarthroplasty treatment options
included core decompression (0.5%), femoral head grafting (0.9%), and proximal femoral
osteotomy (1%).
Etiology and Risk Factors
The etiology and pathophysiology of osteonecrosis is not yet completely understood.
The prevalence of idiopathic NONFH is approximately 15% to 30%.
Multiple risk factors are associated with hip osteonecrosis (Table 1).

Patients with conditions such as systemic lupus erythematous, hematologic
malignancies, and solid organ transplantation and those with HIV have a higher
prevalence of NONFH. The nature of these medical conditions and the frequent use of
glucocorticoids, protease inhibitors (antiretroviral HIV therapy), and chemotherapy are
aggravating and accumulative factors for ONFH.
Natural History
Unmanaged asymptomatic ONFH will progress to symptomatic ONFH and/or collapse in 60%
of patients.
Progression to collapse in approximately 50% of asymptomatic patients10
Large lesions (>50% of the femoral head) have a very high risk for progression (84%).
Medium size lesion (25% to 50% of the femoral head) have a high risk for progression (25%).
Small lesions (<25% of the femoral head) have a low risk for progression (<10%).
Collapse occurs within 2 years in 32% to 79% of patients with symptomatic ONFH.
Core decompression is superior to nonsurgical management in reducing the risk of
progression and collapse in patients with early-stage ONFH.11
Adjuvant cellular therapy may improve the results of core decompression alone; however,
additional studies are necessary.12
Statins improve the results of core decompression alone in patients with steroid-induced
ONFH; however, additional studies are necessary.13
Most patients present with late-stage ONFH (80% to 90%).
THA is the most frequent surgical treatment option in the United States (90%).

Patient History
Patients with ONFH more frequently present in the late stage of the disease, with deep
groin pain as the most common symptom. Pain is worse with activity but may be present
at rest and at night. Contralateral hip pain may be present because bilateral hip disease
is common. Multifocal disease is uncommon; however, surgeons should ask about knee
and shoulder pain.

Imaging Studies
Standing AP and frog-lateral radiographs are the first imaging studies obtained in the
evaluation of young adults in whom ONFH is suspected. In the early stages of ONFH,
radiographs may appear normal. Plain radiographs are helpful in ruling out other causes
of hip pain, such as hip dysplasia, femoroacetabular impingement, and hip osteoarthritis
MRI is the preferred imaging modality for ONFH. The sensitivity and specificity of MRI in
the diagnosis of ONFH are 99%. Focal increases in signal intensity on T2-weighted MRIs
or the presence of a low signal intensity band on T1-weighted MRIs are pathognomonic
findings.
Bone scintigraphy, ultrasonography, positron emission tomography, and dual-energy x-
ray absorptiometry are not recommended for ONFH.

The Modified Ficat and Arlet, the Steinberg, and the ARCO classification systems are the most

and provide information on surgical treatment decision making


Classification Systems
Multiple classifications systems are available to stage ONFH. The most relevant and
frequently cited classification systems include the Modified Ficat and Arlet, the Steinberg
(University of Pennsylvania), and the ARCO staging systems. In 1964, the French
professor Jacques Arlet and Paul Ficat published the first classification system for hip
osteonecrosis. Ficat later modified this classification system in 1985; the modified Arlet
and Ficat classification system is the most frequently cited staging system. Incorporation
of MRI in the evaluation of ONFH allowed for early and accurate diagnosis. It also
allowed for sizing of the necrotic lesion via volumetric or angular measurements. The
Steinberg classification system used MRI to incorporate the size of the lesion and the
extent of head involvement into the different stages of osteonecrosis. The extent of the
lesion in the femoral head and the amount of weight-bearing surface involved determine
the prognosis for the hip.
The ARCO is an international society of expert clinicians and scientists with a focus on
osteonecrosis. The ARCO classification system was developed in 1991 and was updated
in 2019. The final consensus, following an expert panel–based Delphi survey of members
of the ARCO, recommended the use of the revised 2019 ARCO classification as the
universal staging system for ONFH (Resource 4). Determining if the hip has collapsed is
critical. In most patients, THA will be necessary after the hip has collapsed if substantial
pain and disability are present.


Pathology
ONFH is a dynamic process. The morphologic changes vary according to the stage of the
disease. The histopathology can be divided into four stages. The first stage of
osteonecrosis corresponds with the early cellular changes observed after bone death.
The first change is the dissolution of hematopoietic cells, followed by osteocytes
dropping out from the bone lacunae and the presence of bone marrow necrosis. The
second stage occurs several weeks after tissue death. The necrotic fatty marrow shows
dystrophic calcifications, and a reparative process begins at the margin of the necrotic
lesion. The process of appositional new bone formation causes marked thickening of
bone trabeculae. The next stage is the osteoclastic resorption at the viable/necrotic
interface. The resorption process weakens the trabeculae, leading to subchondral
collapse and fracture. Subsequently, necrotic lesion fragmentation, cartilage failure, and
secondary osteoarthritis of the hip occur.

Differential Diagnosis
Transient osteoporosis or bone marrow edema syndrome and femoral neck stress
fractures are conditions that must be differentiated from osteonecrosis of the hip
because of similar presentation. Transient osteoporosis of the hip is an uncommon
cause of hip pain that affects pregnant women and individuals in their forties and fifties.
Transient osteoporosis of the hip is a self-limiting condition that resolves with protected–
weight bearing and analgesic agents. MRI findings include uniform bone marrow edema
of the femoral head, neck, and intertrochanteric region, with increased signal intensity
on T2-weighted MRIs. Transient osteoporosis of the hip lacks the double-density sign
associated with typical hip osteonecrosis.
Femoral neck stress fracture is another potential cause of groin pain. Female patients
and long-distance runners and military recruits with a history of long aerobic exercises
and high-impact activities have an increased risk for stress fractures. The diagnosis is
confirmed via hip MRI. T2-weighted MRIs show a thin, low signal intensity band or line
that corresponds with the fracture line. A marginal high intensity area from the
associated bone marrow edema is observed. Femoral neck stress fractures on the
compression side of the femur are managed nonsurgically, whereas fractures on the
tension side of the bone require surgical fixation to avoid progression to a displaced
femoral neck fracture.
Multiple hip conditions may present as groin pain in young and middle-aged adults.
Structural developmental hip abnormalities, such as acetabular dysplasia and
femoroacetabular impingement are easily differentiated from ONFH. Osteoarthritis,
inflammatory arthritis, septic arthritis, and benign and malignant tumors about the hip
also are potential causes of hip pain.

No role exists for nonsurgical management of ONFH including observation, physical

Hip Preservation Surgery
Core decompression is the most common and accepted treatment option for early-stage
(pre-collapse) ONFH. Core decompression is a conservative surgical technique that has
been performed for decades. It represents a family of procedures that involves creating
a single, large hole or multiple holes in the femoral head. This procedure also may
include débridement of the lesion, adjuvant bone grafting, and cell-based therapy.
Drilling of the femoral head and allograft strut grafting (Phemister technique) was one of
the first known surgical treatment options for ONFH. The work of Ficat on functional
exploration of the bone with bone marrow pressure measurements and femoral head
core biopsy via a small trephine consolidated the terminology and use of core
decompression. The surgical technique is simple and is associated with low morbidity.

Possible explanations are that most patients present with late-stage disease, surgeon

Hip hemiarthroplasty and hemiresurfacing are associated with high failure rates at 10
years and are no longer recommended. The most common reasons for failed
hemiarthroplasty are acetabular erosion and persistent groin pain. Third-generation hip
resurfacing is infrequently performed in the United States because of concerns related
to the generation of metal ions in young patients, corrosion and cobalt-related soft-
tissue reactions.
Higher complication rates, hospital readmission rates, and costs are associated with THA
for ONFH compared with THA for primary osteoarthritis. Regardless, THA is the most
reliable and durable treatment option for late-stage ONFH. The results of THA for ONFH
depend on the underlying diagnosis and the age and activity level of the patient.
